“An age check is just a gate,” sounds narrow. But a gate that asks for proof of who you are is also a filing cabinet with a lock. The law may describe a single doorway; the machinery behind it can become a general-purpose identity system (even if nobody announces that intention). You present a document, a face, or an account, and the service decides whether you may enter. That's not merely a moment of safety. It's a new relationship between your identity and your ordinary online life.

The important question isn't whether a child should be protected. Of course children deserve protection. The question is what happens when every visitor must prove an age before reading, speaking, buying, or searching. Once we've built that checkpoint, we haven't built only a fence around one risky service. We've built a road that other services can use (and governments can ask to inspect). A database assembled for one purpose remains limited to that purpose only because the rule says so. Rules matter, but systems have gravity: once the pipes exist, new water finds them.

You might be told that the check is anonymous. Maybe the system converts your birth date into a yes-or-no token, then discards the original. That can reduce exposure; it doesn't erase the power created by the checkpoint. Someone still decides which proof counts – which vendors may perform the check, and what happens when your device, body, name, or records don't line up. I want to be precise here: a narrower data flow is better than a warehouse of passports. It isn't the same as an identity-free system. The distinction matters because access can be lost without ever seeing the record that made the decision.

For parents, the danger turns a private family judgment into a technical dependency. A parent may decide that your teenager is ready for a particular conversation, game, or health resource. The platform can still say the family's judgment isn't enough. It can demand a credential, route the request through a verifier, and leave parents explaining a denial you can't inspect. A parent who wants safety is then handed a choice between disclosure and exclusion (a bullshit choice, frankly). The system doesn't need to know everything about your child to change the shape of your authority. It only needs to make access conditional.

For privacy advocates, the danger goes beyond a leak. It is the normalization of a demand: show your papers before you participate. We've seen this pattern in other parts of life, where a temporary credential becomes a permanent permission slip (and the people subject to it get fewer ways to say no). We can ask better questions about necessity, retention, appeals, and scope. Parents can insist on trail-free verification, platforms receiving one-time tokens, and failures receiving a clear appeal rather than becoming a silent blacklist. I mean the burden of proof belongs with the system's designers.

I keep returning to a simple test, and I use it whenever a safety promise arrives wrapped around a new checkpoint: after the check is required, can a person still use the service without handing an identity provider a durable relationship to that person? If the answer is no, the policy has crossed from safety measure into infrastructure. A limited design can still create a precedent. You should ask who verifies, what gets stored, who can compel access, how errors are corrected, and whether the system can be used for a new purpose later. If families want safer online spaces, we need boundaries that survive the next emergency. An age gate should block a narrow doorway—not quietly become the building's master key.
